Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
There was an Arab-Islamic intellectual world already dealing with its own questions and its own intense internal conflicts, even as it was also engaging with intellectual sources from outside.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

There is a third issue that matters here when we try to assess the historical importance of the Muʿtazila’s belief in the almost unlimited role of reason in questions of religion, existence, and nature.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Again, we can begin with Ahmed Amin himself.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
He saw one of the Muʿtazila’s weaknesses in the fact that:
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

“They went too far in reasoning from the unseen by analogy with the seen—that is, in comparing God with human beings and subjecting God Almighty to the laws of this world. They required God, for example, to be just according to the human conception of justice and according to justice as a worldly system.”
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
3 — The Meaning of Reasoning from the Seen to the Unseen
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
This is certainly a clear feature of Muʿtazilite thought, especially in the method they used when discussing divine justice.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
But we see another side to it that Ahmed Amin does not.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Although metaphysical questions occupied most of the Muʿtazila’s intellectual activity, their thought never completely lost its roots in material reality—in the seen world.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

This is why, in many Muʿtazilite ideas, theories, and concepts, we have found an underlying recognition of the objective existence of the material world, sometimes implicit and sometimes openly stated.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
None of this, however, took their thinking outside its broadly metaphysical framework.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
When a Muʿtazilite approached questions of divine unity through reason, he still began, above all, from a position of religious faith.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Of course, we should not expect anything very different in that period or in that society.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

The Muʿtazila were innovative thinkers, but they were taking only the first steps toward philosophical thought. In an age and society such as theirs, we cannot expect them to have broken beyond the intellectual limits of their world much further than they actually did. And they had already crossed those limits with unusual courage from the moment they entered the struggle over the basic questions of religious belief.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
But is this philosophical direction alone what determines the Muʿtazila’s place in the history of Arab-Islamic thought?
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
We believe something else is even more decisive. It can be measured historically on the one hand and rationally on the other.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
First, they gave reason a central place in the theory of knowledge.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

They did not separate knowledge from religious faith. Their thought remained within the close connection between knowledge and faith established by Islam. Yet even within that framework, they made reason the primary source of religious knowledge.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

Second, through this philosophical direction, they brought Arab thought into the realm of concepts—that is, into the realm of rational abstraction, which represents a higher form of conscious thought.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī had already taken the first step in this direction, as we saw in our discussion of the Qadarites. But he did not move beyond the simplest stage of abstraction. He did not use philosophical analysis and synthesis in the way the Muʿtazila later did.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
The Muʿtazila developed this method significantly beyond anything that had existed before them.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

They began working with logical categories and philosophical terms such as substance and accident, along with the many rational questions that followed from them. Much of this represented real progress at the theoretical level.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

At the same time, we also find materialist elements appearing within these discussions—sometimes openly, sometimes hidden behind idealist veils that could be thin in one case and much thicker in another.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

The forms of materialism we can discover within Muʿtazilite thought must, of course, be understood in their own historical setting. They had a specifically Islamic religious character. They belonged to a society far removed from our own, one in which religious thought dominated the different forms of intellectual life.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
In this sense, it is right to say that the Muʿtazila were the starting point of Arab-Islamic philosophy.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
The previous chapter also showed how firmly the Muʿtazila held to the principle of causality in explaining events and actions.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
They even connected God’s creation of the world with this principle.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
We also saw that they linked causation in nature with the idea of responsibility at the human and social level, without reducing human action to rigid determinism.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
They distinguished between causation in nature and causation in human action.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Natural causes, they said, operate according to fixed and necessary laws.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Human action includes another element: will.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
This was consistent with their doctrine of human freedom of choice and with the principle on which that doctrine rested: reason.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

The progressive importance of the Muʿtazila’s defence of causality, and of the theoretical arguments they developed around it, becomes clearer when we compare their position with the opposing view that was widespread in their time.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
The Ashʿarites in particular represented this opposing position, and they rejected the principle of causality completely.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Once causality was denied, reason was also pushed out of the field of knowledge, and knowledge became tied entirely to a divine source.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

A comparison between the Muʿtazilite and Ashʿarite positions on causality—and between the theories of knowledge that followed from accepting or rejecting causality—therefore shows the importance of what the Muʿtazila did.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

They confronted an intellectual current that denied the existence of objective laws governing the relationships between things and events throughout the universe. In doing so, that current also denied the possibility that reason could achieve any real independence in knowledge, whatever kind of knowledge was involved.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

The Muʿtazila stood against a current supported at the time by a large body of influential religious thinkers. These included the Ashʿarites, and later sections of the theologians and members of both Sunni and Shiʿi schools.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Despite all their own disagreements, the Muʿtazila were united in confronting this current.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

Their weapon was an advanced body of theoretical thought through which they defended both reason and the principle of causality: causality as a universal law, and also as a rational principle underlying the other objective laws of the universe, nature, and the human world.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
This part of Muʿtazilite thought gives us another element in a scientific historical understanding of their progressive role in intellectual history.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

That role belongs not only to Arab-Islamic history. It can also be placed on the wider level of human intellectual history, because the region in which Muʿtazilite thought flourished later became one of the great centers of scientific thought for a long period during the Middle Ages.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
There is little doubt that the Muʿtazila played an important part in preparing the intellectual conditions that made it possible for this region to become such a major historical center.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
As we saw in the previous chapter, the Muʿtazila made a number of attempts to study the natural world, or the material world more generally.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
But these attempts had a basic weakness.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

They relied almost completely on pure rational thought when studying material phenomena. They did not rely on sensory observation and experiment to discover the general laws governing those phenomena.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

In other words, they did not begin with particular observable cases and things in the material world, study the relationships between them, and then use those relationships to understand natural phenomena and derive general laws.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Instead, they tried to reach such laws through pure reasoning, apart from observing phenomena in their actual movement.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
To put it another way, they relied on abstract logic rather than on the inner, dialectical logic of natural phenomena themselves—the way those phenomena actually move, change, and develop.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
This abstract method led some of them to static conclusions in which nature appeared fixed and motionless, without real change or development.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Their use of abstract logic in studying the natural world therefore created a contradiction between their theory and their practice.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
At the theoretical level, especially in their theory of knowledge, we saw them recognize the relationship between sensory knowledge and rational knowledge.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
They understood that what we perceive through the senses becomes material for rational knowledge.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
We also saw that they reached an essentially sound understanding of how theoretical reason transforms sensory perceptions into rational concepts.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
For thinkers living in their historical circumstances, this was a remarkable achievement.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
But they were unable to apply this theory of knowledge to their own attempts to study nature and the human world.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
We saw this, for example, in their different views on the question of the indivisible substance, or “the part that cannot be divided”—what later became known as the problem of atomism.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
We also saw it in their discussions of substance and accident, motion, and similar questions.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
As for the human world, considered as part of this observable material world, the Muʿtazila discussed many questions involving human action and the physical powers connected with it.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

They did this especially when discussing a person’s capacity to act and trying to define that capacity in physical, spatial, and temporal terms. These questions grew out of their wider discussion of the relationship between God’s power and will and human power and will.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Yet they approached these questions through abstract reasoning in order to build further rational judgments about the relationship between divine power and human power.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
In other words, they were discussing physical and objective questions that really required scientific and experimental investigation.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
We should also keep one important fact in mind.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

What we know of Muʿtazilite thought on these questions comes mostly from sources that were not written by the Muʿtazila themselves. We therefore do not have direct access to the exact methods by which they investigated these issues or argued for their conclusions.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
In later sources—such as al-Ashʿarī, al-Shahrastānī, and others—their views appear broken into pieces and scattered across different discussions, with the connections between them often lost.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
We will explain this and its historical causes below.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
The gap between theory and practice in Muʿtazilite thought had real historical causes.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
The first is something we have already mentioned here and at several points in the previous chapter.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

When the Muʿtazila studied questions concerning nature and the human world, they were usually not studying them for their own sake. They used them mainly as tools for dealing with questions belonging to the world of metaphysics.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Second, the historical conditions of their time did not yet provide them with the experimental means needed to investigate such problems.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
The experimental sciences of nature and humanity had not yet developed far enough in practice to place these tools in the hands of thinkers carrying out theoretical investigations of this kind.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
One exception must be made here: al-Jāḥiẓ.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
He was a Muʿtazilite whom historians regard as the founder of a distinctive tendency within Muʿtazilism and as one of al-Naẓẓām’s most important students.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
He stands apart from the rest of the group because of his experimental tendency and his use of something approaching a scientific method in this field.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Even so, this tendency did not appear as clearly or fully in his Muʿtazilite theological views as it did in his scientific and literary works.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
6 — The Erasure of the Muʿtazilite Heritage
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
There is a well-known historical fact that is both disturbing and difficult to explain.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

Was it merely a coincidence that, not long after the Muʿtazila disappeared from the center of intellectual life during the caliphate of al-Mutawakkil in 847 CE, the original sources of Muʿtazilite thought almost completely disappeared from Arab libraries as well?
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
These were the works and documents in which Muʿtazilite thinkers themselves had set out their ideas and theoretical principles in their own words and in complete form.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
It is difficult for a researcher to believe that some historical accident alone caused such extraordinary damage to thought, knowledge, and history.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

Arab-Islamic intellectual history has certainly seen many tragedies of this kind. But the disappearance of the Muʿtazilite heritage happened under conditions very different from those in which the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage as a whole later began to scatter and disappear.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Why, then, did Muʿtazilite thought alone suffer this fate at a much earlier stage, long before the later conditions that brought destruction to the heritage more generally?
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Perhaps the answer lies in the progressive features of Muʿtazilite thought that we have described throughout the previous two chapters.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
These may have been precisely what led to the sudden disappearance of its heritage from Arab libraries so early in the history of Arab intellectual life.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
A number of conservative intellectual and political currents joined together against the Muʿtazila.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
Their hostility appeared in many forms. The most severe was the almost complete erasure of original Muʿtazilite writings and documents.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five

As a result, only one original source survived into later times: al-Intiṣār by Abū al-Ḥasan al-Khayyāṭ, even though historians of Islamic sects and schools mention many other Muʿtazilite works that remain unknown to us today.
Conclusions from Chapters Four and Five
The destruction of this large and fertile intellectual heritage has prevented us from studying it as a complete and connected body of thought.
